title: Scipio's dream
hook: in Cicero's Dream of Scipio, Rome looks tiny from the stars and fame is short (Republic 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: officium, Cicero's word for a father's duties, built on Panaetius. Your line was on duties. Which one duty did you do well? Day six hundred forty-seven.

Back in year one we spent a day with the pale blue dot, the 1990 photo in which Earth is a speck in a sunbeam. The photo was new. The feeling it gives is not. Everything we fight over, smaller than a grain of dust: about two thousand years before that spacecraft, Cicero wrote it as a dream, in which a young Roman general is lifted among the stars and looks back at his empire. Today: Scipio's dream.
screen: `YEAR ONE: A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.` → `THE FEELING ISN'T NEW.` → `A GENERAL LIFTED TO THE STARS.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. Cicero wrote a book called On the Republic, and ended it with a dream told by Scipio Aemilianus, the general whose circle Panaetius joined. Most of that book was lost for centuries, but the dream survived on its own, because a later writer, Macrobius, wrote a long commentary on it. Second, the dream. Scipio falls asleep and meets his famous grandfather by adoption, Scipio Africanus, the conqueror of Hannibal. Africanus lifts him high among the stars. From there Scipio looks down and the earth is so small that the Roman Empire, which he's spent his life serving, seems a tiny point. He's almost ashamed of it. Third, the lesson about fame. Africanus tells him plainly: your name can't reach most of the earth, much less last. People in other regions will never hear of you. People in later ages will forget. Even the long ages of the sky make human fame seem brief. So don't work for glory. Fourth, what to do instead. Here Cicero adds something Stoic readers will recognize. The dream doesn't say: nothing matters, so do nothing. It says: serve your country well, care for its people, and your reward isn't fame but something higher. In the dream, those who serve well find a place in the heavens. Readers take that differently: some literally, some as poetry. Either way, the view from the stars isn't meant to shrink your effort. It shrinks your need for applause, and leaves the work.
screen: `THE DREAM AT THE END OF A LOST BOOK.` · `FROM THE STARS, ROME IS A POINT.` · `FAME CAN'T REACH FAR OR LAST.` · `SERVE WELL; DROP THE APPLAUSE.` · then, large: `FROM THE STARS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, if you like, and breathe. You've practiced rising above your street before; today go straight to Scipio's height, among the stars, with the earth a small bright point below. Now bring to mind one thing you've wanted credit for lately: a project, a kindness, a clever remark. From up here, how far does word of it travel? A room? A street? Notice what's left when the applause is too small to see: the work itself, and the people it helped. Then come back down, into the room, ready to do the next piece of it. The bell holds the time.
Scipio's dream. In Cicero's dream story, Rome looks tiny from the stars, and fame is short, so serve well without needing the applause. Today's word.
Your line: from the stars. When you catch yourself wanting credit today, rise for one breath, look down, and go back to the work. Day six hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some readers use the Dream of Scipio as an exercise of the imagination, picturing the earth from the stars to loosen the hold of fame, then returning to their work.

fork.setup: you're Scipio, floating among the stars, and your empire looks like a dot. what does Africanus tell you to do?
options: give up public life; none of it matters.
serve your country well, without working for fame.
work harder so your name reaches farther.
fork.reveal: the view from the stars shrinks the need for glory, not the duty. Africanus urges service, with a reward higher than fame.

original.note: Latin: a dream. Somnium Scipionis, the Dream of Scipio, closes Cicero's On the Republic.

trapdoor: what you thought: the view from above is a modern, space-age idea.
what it means: in Cicero's dream, Rome looks tiny from the stars, fame is short, and service still matters.

what a scholar hears: the Somnium Scipionis survived separately through Macrobius's commentary and shaped medieval cosmology; a large part of the rest of De Re Publica was recovered only in 1819 from a palimpsest.

notes: Voyager 1's 'Pale Blue Dot' image, 14 February 1990, from about 6 billion km, beyond Neptune's orbit; Earth less than a pixel. Confirm wording.
Scipio ashamed of the empire's smallness: Republic 6.16. Fame limited in space and time: 6.20–25. Reward for those who serve the state: 6.13, 6.29. Paraphrased; confirm.
De Re Publica palimpsest found by Angelo Mai in the Vatican, published 1822 (discovered 1819). Confirm dates.

Audit (year 2, second sample): the hook retold year one's pale blue dot day (day 123) almost fact for fact, and the rising-above-your-street practice repeated year one's day 122; the hook now names the year-one day in passing and the practice goes to Scipio's height to look at a wish for credit.
